items.reason: Recommend Bardalez Gagliuffi et al. 2025 (ApJL 988, L18), the only solution that includes a direct image of 14 Her c. NASA adopts it for a, e, mass and inclination, and Lu et al. 2026 (arXiv:2605.30177, Table 1) take it as the system's reference parameters. The paper gives a, not P, so P is derived by Kepler III (about 32,900 d, roughly 90 yr).
items.notes: The candidate solutions: (1) Feng et al. 2022 (ApJS 262, 21): P = 15732 +2654/-1896 d, a = 11.92 au, 1597 M-earth. This is the NASA pscomppars P, but its a lies below BG25's 1-sigma range (15.1-32.0 au), and NASA pairs it with BG25's a = 20 au, so the archive row does not hang together. (2) Benedict et al. 2023 (AJ 166, 27; arXiv:2305.11753, abstract): P = 52160 +/- 1028 d, i = 82 +/- 14 deg, M = 7.1 +1.0/-0.6 MJup, from HST FGS + Hipparcos + Gaia + 25 yr of RVs. That P implies a of about 27.3 au for 0.98 M-sun, inside BG25's 1-sigma range. Its quoted +/-1028 d (2%) precision is far tighter than a baseline covering under a fifth of the orbit seems able to support, and BG25 do not adopt it. (3) BG25 (June 2025, refereed ApJL): a = 20.0 +12.0/-4.9 au, e = 0.52, M = 7.9 MJup, i = 116.3 deg, mutual inclination 32 deg. I recommend BG25 because it is the most recent refereed fit and the only one with relative astrometry of c itself. Lu et al. 2026 (arXiv:2605.30177, submitted June 2026, not yet refereed) is a dynamics paper that re-uses BG25's parameters and gives no new orbit. I found no second-epoch JWST orbit. P is poorly constrained whichever solution is used. Writing the derived P with an orange border and the WEAK tag is the honest representation.

items.notes: What is actually measured: JWST images give the planet's position on the sky (MIRI discovery epoch, Matthews et al. 2024; NIRCam epoch, Sanghi et al. 2026). That is combined with 29 years of host-star RVs and the Hipparcos-Gaia proper-motion anomaly. Together they yield a dynamical (true, not m sin i) mass, with a, e and i fitted. P is only a derived parameter (from a and total mass), and the data cover under half an orbit, so P, a and e are loosely constrained. The brief asks for 'the 2024 JWST-era solution' (Matthews et al. 2024, Nature 633, 789). The NASA ps row for it gives a 28.4 au, e 0.40, 2005.5 M-earth (6.31 MJup) and no P. I recommend against it: the same group's 2026 refits supersede it. Sanghi et al. show that unmodelled activity and RV stitching biased earlier eccentricities (abstract). Matthews et al. 2026 (arXiv:2603.08780, Table 3, accepted to ApJL, ps default_flag 0) get P 108 +49/-25 yr, a 20.9 +5.8/-3.3 au, e 0.244, 7.63 MJup, and attribute the change to the perspective-acceleration treatment. The two 2026 fits differ by roughly 1-sigma in a. Sanghi is chosen because it is the refereed journal paper, the NASA default, and includes the newer NIRCam astrometry. Sanghi's fiducial host mass is 0.80 M-sun; the Systems tab has 0.762.

items.reason: The 4386 M-earth (13.8 MJup) and 'likely BD' come from Vanderburg et al. 2020, whose 13.8 MJup is a 95% upper limit, not a mass. Two JWST papers since then call it a planet: Limbach et al. 2025 (MIRI emission, no more than ~6 MJup) and MacDonald et al. 2026 (Nature, NIRSpec), the first direct mass constraint, 4.3-10.9 MJup. Replace the mass and drop the 'likely BD' flag.
items.notes: Stale flag cells: Planets within 100 ly row 517 'Orbit data source / flags' ('OEC 2026-07-31; >13 MJ - likely BD'); Systems within 100 ly row 11 'Planet masses (M-earth)'; Multi-stars within 100 ly rows 76, 77 and 78 'Planet masses (M-earth)' (the same text repeated on the WD row and both G 229-20 companion rows). I checked every cell on every tab whose row mentions WD 1856 for 'BD'/'brown dwarf' and found only these five. Row 517's 'Mass (M-Jup)' (13.80) and 'OEC mass (M-Jup) -- cross-check' / 'Mass agreement' cells will change with the mass. The two JWST papers disagree. Limbach et al. 2025 (arXiv:2504.16982, Table 1 and Sect. IV.3) measure a 186 K mid-IR brightness temperature and, from cooling models, 5.2 +0.7/-0.8 MJup if insolation is negligible, or 0.84-5.9 MJup otherwise; NASA ps holds this as 1652.7 M-earth, default_flag 0. MacDonald et al. 2026 (published in Nature, 1 Jul 2026) retrieve the mass from the spectrum's scale height, find a nightside T_eff of 390-412 K, and so argue for a later reheating event, which undercuts a passive-cooling mass. I recommend MacDonald as the latest refereed and more direct constraint. Because the paper gives a range, not one adopted value, confidence is medium; Limbach's 5.2 MJup (1652.7 M-earth) is the alternative. Either way the planet is below 13 MJup at 1 sigma, though MacDonald note it 'may be above ... 13 MJ within 2 sigma'. The flags text says so, so the row does not swing from 'likely BD' to certainly-planet. Leave P, a, e and R as Vanderburg's, consistent with the sheet's 0.52 M-sun host mass; Limbach's a = 0.02085 au uses a 0.605 M-sun white dwarf.
